header.tag_why: The evaluation started with store returns and split customer records, and 11 of the 14 follow-up questions were about stores; it was lost at the store ops workshop, where we described a till return instead of showing one and offered a partner for installs, while Adyen brought people who had done store rollouts.

evidence.excerpt: Returns. Last holiday season. Buy online, return in store.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: The store couldn't see the online order, so staff were refunding to gift cards or telling people to mail it back.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: they'd just launched a loyalty program that was supposed to work everywhere and didn't, because store and web were two different customer records.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Their COO, Angela, apparently stood in a store on December 27th watching the returns queue. That's the story everybody there tells.
evidence.label: opinion

trigger.insight: The trigger was a store-operations failure (returns at the till and a broken loyalty program), and the story everyone there tells puts the COO in the returns queue, not anyone from the web team. Our web checkout strength did not touch the pain that started this deal, so we were solving a problem the customer did not open the evaluation for.
trigger.messaging: For omnichannel retailers, open with the buy-online-return-in-store scenario and one customer record across store and web, not with checkout conversion.

evidence.label: fact

evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Once. The kickoff.
evidence.label: fact

decider.insight: Tom first named Raj, then admitted that Angela signed with Adyen, and that he met her only once, at the kickoff. Running the RFP made Raj our contact, but the person who owned the pain made the decision, and her team asked for the stores workshop where the deal turned. Raj's support rests only on his own word to Tom.
decider.messaging: Our retail messaging and proof need to speak to the COO / store-ops buyer (accountability, rollout, the till), not only to the CTO.

evidence.label: fact

evidence.label: fact

evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Raj forwarded me a list of 14 questions and 11 of them were about stores.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: As Raj relayed it, Adyen sold people and accountability: a team that had done store rollouts, one contract, and references the COO recognized. They did not win on features. After that meeting the customer's questions moved from web to stores (wifi drops, a 120-store rollout, who shows up on a Saturday), so Adyen set the evaluation criteria and we answered on their terms.
competitor.messaging: Lead unified commerce with who does the rollout and who answers when a till fails, plus named retail references, rather than with the platform claim.

evidence.excerpt: Reaction: the online checkout demo. Their ecommerce lead loved it. The wallets, the one-click piece.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Silence: the unified commerce part.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's a diagram.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then she asked how a return works. Step by step. At the till.
evidence.label: fact

message.insight: The part of the pitch that landed (checkout, wallets) reached the ecommerce lead, who was not the buyer. The part aimed at the actual pain, M3 almost word for word, got silence, and the head of store operations dismissed it as "that's a diagram." M3 states the line between online and in-store has disappeared, but it does not prove it; the store buyer wanted the steps of one return at the till, and we had no answer beyond describing it.
message.messaging: Replace M3's abstract claim with a concrete walkthrough: an online order returned at a store till, refund to the original card, same customer record.

evidence.excerpt: They had six people from store operations. Nobody on our side had run a store rollout.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: When Bev asked who does the installs, I said we'd bring in a partner. She wrote something down and didn't ask another question.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I knew on the drive home.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: Right before that, honestly, we were ahead. Raj said so. We'd won the web side.
evidence.label: opinion

decided.insight: The deal turned at the stores workshop, and the partner answer on installs contradicted the COO's stated fear, "I don't want two vendors pointing at each other." The sense that we were ahead rested on Raj's word and on the web side only, even though the questions had already shifted to stores by then. We were ahead on a dimension the decider was not scoring.
decided.messaging: Where we rely on install partners, message a single point of accountability across partner and platform, and staff store workshops with people who have done store rollouts.

evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Then a rollout plan. Dates, who installs, what happens to the old tills.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They wanted to watch an online order get returned at a store till, live. We described it. We never showed it.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: All three gaps were proof gaps: a reference call, a rollout plan, and a live return at a till. A case study did not meet the COO's need for proof when Adyen had named retailers she knew. The transcript does not say whether we could have shown the live return; it only says we never did, so whether this is a product gap or a demo-readiness gap is unclear.
gaps.messaging: Back M8 for retail with reference customers ready to take a call and a standard live till-return demo, instead of written case studies.

language.insight: The customer framed the problem as accountability and a single customer: one system, one customer, one basket, no finger-pointing between vendors. We framed it as product categories (unified commerce, in-person payments, point of sale), and Tom says they never once used "unified commerce." Adyen's reported pitch, one platform for the tills and the website on one contract, was close to Bev's own phrase.
language.messaging: Rewrite M3 in the customer's words: "One system for the tills and the website" with "one customer, one basket", one contract, and one team accountable.

gaps.question: Who made the final call, and how do you know?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: what evidence beyond the signature shows how Angela weighed the decision, and did Raj ever tell you directly that he recommended us to her?

gaps.question: What did Adyen actually present, and on what contract terms?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Raj (via Tom): could he share Adyen's rollout plan or who was on their retail team? Also request a loss interview with Angela or Bev to hear it firsthand.

gaps.question: Could we have shown a live online-to-till return, and could we have committed to a rollout plan with dates and installs?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the solutions engineer who attended the workshop: was the live return demo technically possible at that point, and what blocked a rollout plan?

gaps.question: Why couldn't a reference call be set up in time?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom and customer marketing: which retail references were available, and what was the lead time?

gaps.question: What did the customer use before (incumbent for tills and web)?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Tom: what payment providers did Marlowe & Finch run in stores and online before this RFP?

close.rep_takeaway: The person running the RFP is not always the person who decides: here the pain belonged to the COO, her team asked for the workshop where the deal turned, and she signed, after we had met her once. When the customer's questions shift (11 of 14 about stores), treat it as a signal that the buyer has changed, get in front of that person, and bring proof (a live demo, a reference call, a rollout plan) instead of describing it.
